working: White is where your rating comes from, and the gap widened. 57% as White against 44% as Black across all 213 rated games — thirteen points, where this page reported nine a week ago. That reading has now been eleven, then nine, then thirteen across three updates, so treat the exact figure as noisy; the direction has never once changed. These remain the two largest samples on the page.

The Stonewall Attack is still your most reliable opening. 67% across 15 games against a 51% overall average. You played it three times this week for two wins and a loss and the score did not move at all. The Englund scores higher at 73% across 11 games, but on a much smaller sample. Games 49 and 55 were both decided by the same Ne5, Bxe5, fxe5 structure you have played dozens of times — it is the one line where the plan is in place before the position turns sharp.

An eight-game unbeaten run, the best stretch in this list. Games 38 through 45 went seven wins and a draw and carried you from 1329 to 1385, the highest you have stood since the run that set the 1410 peak. Two of those wins came against opponents rated well above you, including the 1456 in Game 45. You gave most of it back afterwards but still finished the week at 1349.

Your first game of a session is still your best game. 55% across 99 first-games, ahead of every later slot and built on the largest sample here. The shape of the decline after it has shifted again though — see opposite.

Finishing attacks with checkmate. Games 6, 7, 12, 14, 21, 23, 28, 32 and now 41, 42 and 43 all ended in forced mate rather than material collection. Game 41 is the clearest of them: he spent moves 13 and 14 taking a pawn and then a rook on f1 while you played 13.Ng5 and 14.Qxh5, and 15.Qh7# landed before any of it mattered.
watch: Short games got worse this week, not better. 42 games have now ended under 20 moves, up from 38 a week ago, scoring 36% for a net of −157 rating points. Three of the four new ones were losses: Game 50 at nineteen moves, Game 57 at seventeen, Game 61 at fifteen. Everything longer is close to break-even, so this one bucket is still the whole difference between a flat 18 months and a climbing one.

The habit is not tracking what his pieces already touch. The old examples all involved blocking a check — Game 24's ...b5 onto a square the d4 knight covered, Game 26's ...c6, Game 18's 10.Qb4??. This week it appeared twice with no check involved at all. Game 50: your knight on d4 was the only thing between his bishop on b2 and your queen on e5, 16...Nxe2+ moved it, and 18.Bxe5 took the queen. Game 61: 7.Bd5 attacked the rook on a8 the moment the b-pawn left b7, 8...b4 ignored it, 9.Bxa8. Name every enemy piece that touches the square you are leaving as well as the one you are going to.

Black is where the losses are, and it is costing more than before. 44% as Black against 57% as White. Every one of this week's six Philidor losses came as Black, and so did three of the four new short games. One solid, properly-learned answer to 1.e4 is still the single highest-value thing you could study.

The session curve held its shape, and the cliff is still at five. It now reads 55%, 51%, 45% and 53% across games one through four, then 31% from the fifth game on. The fourth-game figure rose a little and the fifth-and-later figure slipped a little, so the earlier correction stands: four games is the ceiling, not two. That last row still rests on only 16 games, which is small — the drop is real, its size is not yet trustworthy.

The Philidor has now dipped below your own average. 48% across 56 games against 51% overall, down from the 51% this page reported last week. It was also your most-played line of the week and the source of most of the damage: Games 48, 50, 52, 57, 59 and 61 were all Philidor losses, and two of those were the Exchange Variation, which has now beaten you in Games 13, 20, 50 and 57. This page has said four different things about the Philidor as the sample grew; the honest reading is that it is an ordinary opening for you that went through a bad week.

Van't Kruijs is still the worst result on the board: 25% across 8 games, with the Indian Defence next at 39% over 9. You played neither this week, so both figures are exactly where they were — and both samples are still small enough that luck could account for them. Worth studying or dropping rather than continuing to find out slowly.
